title: The last thought
hookLine: a king gave up his throne to meditate, then spent his last breath thinking about a baby deer
carry: the last thought is made of every day

cards: A king named Bharata gave up his kingdom and went to live by a river in the forest, to spend his days in prayer. That's how the Bhagavata Purana tells it.
One day a pregnant deer, frightened by a lion's roar, leapt the river, gave birth, and died. The fawn was left alone. Bharata took it in.

He fed it, worried about it, went looking for it when it wandered. Little by little the fawn filled his whole mind. And when Bharata died, the story says, the last thing he was thinking about was the deer.
Today's verses say the same thing plainly.

teach.h: WHAT FILLS THE MIND SHAPES WHERE YOU GO.
teach.b: In the story, Bharata is reborn as a deer. The story doesn't tell it as a punishment. It reads like Gita 8.6 made into a picture: what fills the mind shapes where a person goes.
The story goes on; he keeps the memory of his past life, and in his next birth he finally reaches the goal. Chapter eight, verses eight to sixteen, describe the other way to die.
Meditate on the ancient seer, the ruler, finer than the finest, who holds everything up, whose form can't be imagined, bright as the sun beyond darkness.

teach.h: OM, AND THE BREATH BETWEEN THE BROWS.
teach.b: At the time of departure, verse ten says, with a steady mind and devotion, draw the breath up between the brows.

Verse thirteen gives the single syllable to hold: speaking Om, which is Brahman, and remembering Krishna, the one who leaves the body goes to the highest goal. Then verse fourteen, and here's the gentleness.

teach.h: EASY TO REACH, FOR THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS.
teach.b: For the one who always remembers me, every day, with a mind that goes nowhere else, I am easy to reach. Sulabha: easily attained.
The great souls who come to Krishna, verse fifteen says, don't come back to this temporary home of sorrow. So the last thought isn't really about the last moment.
You can't cram for it. Bharata had given up everything else, and a fawn still filled his mind, because it's what he'd thought about every day.

teach.h: THE LAST THOUGHT IS BEING WRITTEN NOW.
teach.b: The last thought is made of all the ordinary ones, and it's being written now, one day at a time.

how: Some Hindus chant Om or a divine name every day, in the hope that it will be what comes to mind at the end.

o: rare and very hard to find

games.q: who and what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the king who left his throne
filled his mind at the end

s: the Gita says you can cram for your last thought
the last thought is made of the everyday ones; 8.14 says God is easy to reach for the one who always remembers.
in the story, Bharata's last thought was of a deer
he was reborn as a deer, keeping his memory, and later reached the goal.
verse 13 names Om as the syllable that is Brahman
speaking Om, the one syllable, and remembering Krishna.

games.q: you're Bharata, living alone in the forest to pray. a mother deer dies, and her newborn fawn is left alone. what do you do?
o: leave it; nature will take its course.
take it in and raise it.
give it to a nearby village.
games.why: he raises it, and grows so attached that the fawn fills his last thought. the story is told to show how the everyday mind becomes the final one.

practice: Sit tall, let the breath settle, and hold the one syllable verse thirteen gives: if you're comfortable with it, hum a long, quiet Om on the out-breath; if not, simply let the breath out slowly through the nose.
Either way, rest in the silence after it, then breathe in again, a few times over. Notice how easily the sound comes back once it's been practiced.

wordCard.voice: Sulabha. Easy to reach: what Krishna says of himself to the one who always remembers. Gita chapter eight: what you remember at the end is what you've been remembering all along.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sulabha, easy to reach (8.14); su (easy) + labha (gaining).

carryVoice: Your line: the last thought is made of every day. For the one who remembers every day, Krishna is easy to reach. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 5.7–5.9 (King Bharata and the deer)
